summary: The Taikon 5 is the first model from Forthing, a Dongfeng sub-brand distributed in Australia by Ateco, and since September 2026 it has been marketed here simply as the Forthing Electric because Porsche has opposed the Taikon trademark; cars still wear the badge and the dispute is unresolved. Both battery-electric grades share one 150kW front-drive motor and a 64.4kWh LFP pack rated at 427km WLTP, so the Luxury-to-Exclusive step buys equipment rather than range, and a range-extender version of the same body is sold alongside and excluded here. Australian reviewers agree it is sharply priced, roomy and efficient (CarExpert saw 14.1 to 15.0kWh/100km indicated), but rate its front-drive dynamics from below average to poor, with torque steer, a jittery or floaty ride and modest tyre grip.
pros: Among the cheapest mid-size electric SUVs in Australia at $38,990 drive-away for the Luxury, about $6,000 under a GAC Aion V Premium and $9,500 under a Leapmotor C10 Style on a comparable drive-away basis
Efficient for the class: CarExpert recorded 14.1 to 15.0kWh/100km indicated on test, against Forthing's 15.5kWh/100km claim
480-litre boot (Forthing's figure, excluding underfloor storage) expanding to 1480 litres, against 427/978 litres for a GAC Aion V and 300/1079 litres for a Chery E5

Unconditional seven-year/200,000km vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing strings, plus an eight-year/200,000km battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent capacity; roadside assistance extends to five years only if every scheduled service is done at a Forthing service centre

Base Luxury already includes a 14.6-inch screen, wireless CarPlay and Android Auto, 10-way power driver's seat with ventilation and massage, 19-inch alloys, 3.5kW V2L, AEB, adaptive cruise and blind-spot monitoring, and the Exclusive adds a space-saver spare that is rare on an EV
cons: Unrated by ANCAP, and the car ships without driver-attention monitoring or e-call, which rules out a five-star result under the current protocol
Forthing's October 2026 spec sheet rates it to tow only 750kg braked or unbraked, half the 1500kg a Leapmotor C10 is rated for and half the figure Forthing published at launch
80kW peak DC charging is slow for the segment, giving 30-80 per cent in about 30 minutes against roughly 24 minutes for 10-80 per cent on a 180kW GAC Aion V
Front-drive dynamics draw the reviews' main criticism: EV Central cites torque steer, vague steering, body float and motor whine, and CarExpert calls it quick to reach its limits on budget tyres

A new brand with 26 dealers nationally (seven in Victoria), a naming dispute with Porsche that may yet force a rename, and drive-away-only pricing with no published list price, so resale is entirely unproven
